summary: This informational document is a framework for time-scheduled reservation of traffic engineering resources. It can provide resource booking for TE LSPs, improving guarantees for customers and efficiency of network usage over time.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8413 describes a way to reserve network capacity for a future time instead of asking for it at the moment it is needed. A central controller computes the path in advance and records the booking, then signals the tunnel when the booked time arrives. The document is a framework: it sets out the design and says nothing about the protocols that would carry it.

questions: how to book network resources in advance
how does a pce schedule lsps
why keep scheduling state in a central pce
subtitle: How to book network capacity for a future time slot, and still signal the tunnel only when it is needed.

tldr.problem: An operator often knows that a tunnel will be needed at a particular time, but computing a path today gives no guarantee the capacity will be free then, and setting the tunnel up early wastes capacity in the meantime.
tldr.mechanism: A Path Computation Element keeps a time-based view of network resources and a database of planned tunnels, computes the path in advance and holds the resources for a future window, and signals the tunnel only when its start time arrives.
tldr.outcome: The RFC gives an architecture and the reasoning behind it. It defines no protocol and no protocol extension, so the pieces have to be built elsewhere.

today: RFC 8413 is an Informational document from July 2018 that no RFC obsoletes or updates. Because it defines no protocol, it is a reference for design work rather than a specification to implement.

sections.title: Why Schedule Resources in Advance
sections.content:
Traffic Engineering Label Switched Paths (TE-LSPs) are connection-oriented tunnels in packet and non-packet networks. They may reserve network resources for the traffic they carry, which gives some guarantee of service delivery and lets an operator plan resource use across the whole network. In some technologies, such as wavelength switched optical networks, the resource is the label switched on the path, so an LSP cannot exist without a physical resource assigned to it. In packet switched networks, the resource assigned to an LSP is a measure of the link capacity dedicated to the traffic on that LSP.

Network planning means choosing paths so that no two LSPs contend for the same resources. LSP establishment is the act of setting up an LSP and reserving resources; network optimization or reoptimization is repositioning LSPs so that the unreserved resources are more useful for future LSPs while the established ones keep meeting their objectives.

TE resources are reserved at the point of use. The resources, such as wavelengths, timeslots or bandwidth, are reserved on a specific link and tracked by the Label Switching Routers (LSRs) at the ends of that link, which learn what to reserve during LSP setup. Resources held for one LSP may be preempted for another. With RSVP-TE signaling, a holding priority and a preemption priority decide which LSP may preempt which; with direct central control, the controller makes the decision. Operator policy is a key part of preemption, because there is a trade-off between disrupting existing LSPs and enabling new ones.

Paths are usually computed in full ahead of setup, either by the head-end LSR or by Path Computation Element (PCE) functionality in a dedicated server or in network management software, so that an end-to-end view of available resources can be used. Even then two LSPs set up at the same time may compete for scarce resources and one or both may fail, which a centralized PCE that knows about requests in progress avoids. Path computation is subject to objective functions, which may be criteria about the LSP itself, such as the shortest path to the destination, or about the network state afterwards, such as maximized residual link bandwidth. The requester may ask for an objective function, and the computation engine may filter and enhance it according to operator policy.
sections.plainLanguage: An LSP is a tunnel that reserves capacity along a path, and the network has to fit those reservations without two tunnels fighting over the same capacity. Today a tunnel is normally set up when it is needed, and the path is worked out just before that. This RFC asks what changes when the operator already knows the tunnel will be needed later.

sections.title: Planning Future LSPs and Future Demands
sections.content:
It is often known in advance that an LSP will be needed at a particular time, for example a large traffic flow that starts at a well-known time, perhaps for database synchronization or for content exchange between streaming sites. The requester may also know for how long the LSP is required before it can be torn down.

One approach is to collect the requests for future LSPs in a central database, such as at a Network Management System (NMS), and ask the PCE to compute a path when the time comes. The document lists the drawbacks: it is not possible to determine in advance whether the LSP can be delivered, because the resources it needs might be used by other LSPs in the meantime, so at the time the request is made the NMS can make only a best-effort guarantee.

The better solution is to service the requests for future LSPs at once. The paths are computed ahead of time and converted into reservations of network resources during specific windows in the future: while the path is computed and the resources are reserved, the LSP is not established in the network until the time for which it is scheduled. This also allows a commitment to be made to a service user that an LSP will be set up and available at a specific time. The document calls this Time-Scheduled TE (TS-TE) resource reservation, achieved by tracking the current use of network resources and also having a future view of resource usage.

Path computation that looks only at current resources cannot handle every case. It is easy to construct scenarios where LSPs placed one at a time block a later LSP, although foreknowledge of all the LSPs would have made it possible to set them all up.

Scheduled and unplanned reservations coexist. When an unplanned LSP is requested, no prior accommodation can be made, so it can be placed no better than it would be without TS-TE, but it can be placed taking the future demands of already requested TS-TE LSPs into account. Since the unplanned LSP has no known end time, any network planning must assume it consumes resources forever.
sections.plainLanguage: The argument for booking ahead is simple. A path computed today says nothing about whether the capacity will still be free next Tuesday, and reserving the capacity today blocks it from being used for something else in between. Computing the path in advance and holding the capacity for a named window fixes both problems.

sections.title: The Scheduling State and the Two Databases
sections.content:
The scheduling state indicates when resources are reserved and when they are available for use. The simple information model for one piece of it holds a link id, a resource id or reserved capacity, a reservation start time and a reservation end time. The resource that is scheduled could be link capacity, physical resources on a link or buffers on an interface, and could include advanced considerations such as CPU utilization and memory availability at nodes. The resource information might also include the maximal unreserved bandwidth of the link over a time interval, which would book a percentage of the residual bandwidth of the link, for example to reserve bandwidth for a traffic class that has no provisioned LSP. For any one resource there could be multiple pieces of scheduling state, and for any one link the timing windows might overlap. The state could be expressed as a start time and an end time or as a start time and a duration, multiple reservation periods of different lengths may need to be recorded for each resource, and the current state of network reservation could be kept separate from the scheduled usage or merged into a single database. A single reservation request may book resources for multiple periods and may ask for a reservation that repeats on a regular cycle.

Two databases are needed. The first is an enhanced, time-based Traffic Engineering Database (TED) that stores traffic engineering information, such as bandwidth, for every link over a series of time intervals. If the unreserved bandwidth at a priority level for a link is Bj in the interval from Tj to Tk, the TED can store it as [T0, B0], [T1, B1], [T2, B2], [T3, B3] and so on.

The second is an LSP Database (LSP-DB) that holds information not only about LSPs active in the network but also about planned ones. For each time interval that applies to the LSP, the entry holds the interval, the paths computed for the LSP that satisfy the constraints in that interval, and the resources, such as bandwidth, reserved in that interval. The information about future LSPs has to be stored separately from the resource scheduling, so that the LSPs can be instantiated when they are due and use the paths and resources computed for them, and so that it is clear why resources were reserved. That correlation is what makes preemption and the release of reserved resources possible when a future LSP is canceled. If the bandwidth reserved for an LSP on a link was B from time T2 to T3, and the unreserved bandwidth on that link in that interval was B2, then on cancellation B is added back and the unreserved bandwidth becomes B2 + B. It is an implementation choice how the TED and LSP-DB are stored for dynamic use and for recovery, and all the information in the scheduled TED can be recovered from the active network state and from the scheduled LSP-DB.
sections.plainLanguage: The scheduling state records, for each piece of capacity, when it is booked and when it is free. Two records are kept at the controller: a time-based view of how much capacity each link has left in each interval, and a list of the tunnels that have been planned, with the path and the capacity each one holds. The second record is what lets the controller give the capacity back when a planned tunnel is cancelled.

sections.title: Where the Scheduling State Is Held
sections.content:
The scheduling state has to be held somewhere, and the document considers two places: in the network nodes where the resources exist, or in a central scheduling controller where decisions about resource allocation are made.

Holding it in the network nodes makes policing of resource allocation easier, because many points in the network can request immediate or scheduled LSPs and all such requests can be correlated where the resources are allocated. But there are scaling and technical problems. Each node must retain the full time-based state for all of its resources, and in a busy network with a high arrival rate of new LSPs and a low hold time for each, that is a lot of state on nodes normally built with minimal spare memory. The PCE needs a database of available links and nodes, the TED, usually populated from information advertised in the IGP or exported using BGP-LS (BGP Link State); to compute a path for a future LSP the PCE must populate the TED with all of the future resource availability, and if that information is held on the nodes it must also be advertised in the IGP, where all the advertised information is held at every node and must be refreshed periodically. A restarted node recovers reservation state from forwarding hardware, from non-volatile memory, or from adjacent nodes through the signaling protocol, but scheduling state held at the nodes would also have to be recovered after a restart, which cannot be done from the forwarding hardware because the reservation has not been made, might need expensive non-volatile memory, or might require the adjacent nodes to hold the scheduling state too so that it can be reinstalled.

Holding the state centrally means it is easily available at the point of use: the PCE can use it to plan future LSPs and update it with the scheduled reservation of resources. Central holding has its own issues. Multiple controllers must synchronize their stored scheduling state as they plan, and must have a mechanism to resolve contention, which is mitigated by the ample time available to replan. If other sources of immediate LSPs are allowed, the changes in resource availability they cause must be reflected in the TED and may affect planned future LSPs, which can be mitigated by replanning or by preemption. The state must be held and restored after a system restart, which is relatively easy on a central server with non-volatile storage. And a centralized system must store information about all the resources in the network, which multiplied by the size of the network and the number of trackable resources on each link or at each node is a lot of state. That last challenge is only solved if the central server has full control of booking resources and establishing new LSPs, so that the information from the network only confirms what the server expected.

The architectural conclusion is that the scheduling state should be held centrally at the point of use and not in the network devices.

Operator policy runs through the design. A PCE may refuse a computation request because the application lacks permission or because servicing it would take resource use over a threshold. Preemption and holding priorities may be rejected or overwritten by policy, and objective functions are usually selected by the PCE or the management system rather than by the application. An operator might want only a certain percentage of any resource to be bookable, and might want preemption of booked resources to be an inverse function of how far in the future the resources are needed for the first time. The granularity of the timing window offered to an application also depends on operator policy and defines the operator's service offerings.
sections.plainLanguage: The document weighs putting the booking records in the routers against putting them in a central controller, and settles on the controller. The routers would have to hold and advertise a time-based view of their own capacity, which does not scale, and recovering that state after a router restart would be hard. A central controller keeps one copy and can plan against it.

sections.title: The Lifecycle of a Scheduled LSP
sections.content:
The reference architecture has a Service Requester, a PCE holding an LSP-DB and a TED, and the network. The Service Requester may be an application, a network management system, an LSR, or any component that qualifies as a Path Computation Client. It sends a request to the PCE for an LSP to be set up at some time, either now or in the future, including all the parameters the requester wishes to supply, such as priority, bandwidth, start time and end time.

The PCE enters the request in its LSP-DB and uses information from its TED to compute a path that satisfies the constraints, such as bandwidth, for the whole interval from the start time to the end time. It updates the future resource availability in the TED, so that further path computations can take the scheduled usage into account, and stores the computed path in the LSP-DB.

When it is time for the LSP to be set up, the PCE sends a PCEP Initiate request to the head-end LSR, giving the path to be signaled and the other parameters such as the bandwidth. As the LSP is signaled between LSRs, the use of resources in the network is updated and distributed using the IGP; this information reaches the PCE through the IGP or through BGP-LS, and the PCE updates its TED. After the LSP is set up, the head-end LSR sends a PCEP LSP State Report (PCRpt) message to the PCE containing the resources, such as bandwidth usage, for the LSP, and the PCE updates the status of the LSP in the LSP-DB. When the LSP is no longer required, either because the requester canceled it or because its scheduled lifetime expired, the PCE instructs the head-end LSR to tear it down, the network resource usage is updated by the IGP and advertised back, and the PCE removes the LSP from the LSP-DB.

Depending on operator policy, and to minimize network perturbations, the PCE may reoptimize the LSPs it has computed paths for when the TED is updated. For LSPs that are already provisioned it issues PCEP Update request messages; for scheduled LSPs that have not yet been provisioned it updates the stored plan instead. Reoptimization is subject to operator oversight, because frequent changes affect the stability of the network.

When a PCE is initialized it must learn the state from the network, from its stored databases and possibly from other PCEs. It first needs an accurate view of topology and resource availability, normally by reading the state directly from the network via the IGP or BGP-LS, or possibly by receiving a copy of the TED from another PCE; a TED stored from a previous instantiation is unlikely to be valid. It then constructs the time-based TED, either by recovering one saved to non-volatile storage or by reconstructing it from the LSP-DB saved there. The LSP-DB needs to hold both the intended and the actual state of LSPs so that a recovered PCE can determine what actions are necessary. If more than one PCE supports scheduling, they must synchronize their scheduled TED and scheduled LSP-DB. The options are a shared database driven by all the PCEs, which is likely to be inefficient and hard to interoperate, a distributed database synchronization mechanism with each PCE responsible for its own scheduled database, which is efficient but still hard to interoperate across heterogeneous implementations, or PCEP messages used to synchronize scheduled state, which works well when the number of PCEs is small but needs considerable message exchange as the number grows.

Multi-domain operation needs cooperation between PCEs, each responsible for a segment of the end-to-end path, and resources must be booked in every domain the path crosses. Per-domain path computation is not appropriate for a scheduled LSP, because the requests at downstream PCEs are only triggered by signaling, but a similar mechanism could be used where cooperating PCEs exchange Path Computation Request messages for a scheduled LSP, with the upstream PCE computing a path across its domain, reserving the resources and asking the downstream PCE to compute and reserve in the other domain; the downstream PCE may return a full path or a path key. Backward Recursive PCE-Based Computation (BRPC) can arrive at a more optimal end-to-end path, but it suits scheduling poorly, because the downstream PCE would have to reserve resources on all of the potential paths and then release the ones the upstream PCE did not use. A hierarchical PCE, in which a parent PCE coordinates the requests to the child PCEs, gives better visibility of the end-to-end path and better coordination of the booking.
sections.plainLanguage: The sequence is: a requester asks for a tunnel with a start and end time, the controller works out a path and marks the capacity as booked, and nothing is signaled yet. When the start time arrives, the controller tells the entry router to set the tunnel up, the routers report the capacity they used, and the controller records that. At the end of the window the controller tells the entry router to tear the tunnel down and releases the booking.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The protocol implications of scheduled resources are unchanged from on-demand LSP computation and setup. Securing PCEP is discussed in RFC 5440, with work to extend that security in RFC 8253, and the path key mechanism of RFC 5520 can be used to enhance privacy and security. There is also no change to the security implications for the signaling of scheduled LSPs; the security of the signaling protocols that would be used is discussed in RFC 5920.

What does change is the size of the window in which an attack can be started or planned. Scheduled LSPs give a logically infinite window. If bogus scheduled LSPs can be requested and entered into the LSP-DB, then a large number of LSPs could be launched and significant network resources blocked. The document therefore says that control of scheduling requests needs to be subject to operator policy, that additional authorization needs to be applied for access to LSP scheduling, and that diagnostic tools need to be provided to inspect the LSP-DB to spot attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: Booking capacity in advance does not change how the signalling or the controller protocol are secured. It does, however, give an attacker a much longer window to plan an attack, since reservations can be made far into the future. The document therefore asks for authorization on scheduling requests and for tools to inspect the planned-tunnel database.

messages.note: Sent when the request is canceled or the scheduled lifetime expires.

viz.caption: TWO PLACES TO KEEP THE SCHEDULING STATE

items.title: One reservation
items.text: Link id, resource id or reserved capacity, reservation start time, reservation end time.

items.title: Time-based TED
items.text: Unreserved bandwidth for every link over a series of intervals, stored as [T0, B0], [T1, B1] and so on.

items.title: LSP-DB
items.text: For each time interval: the interval, the computed paths, and the resources reserved for that LSP.

items.title: Why both
items.text: The TED alone cannot release the right capacity when a planned LSP is canceled.
